title: How should you answer when an interviewer asks why consulting, and why their firm?
description: How to give specific, believable answers to the two motivation questions every consulting interviewer asks, with an example structure.
hook: Answer "why consulting" with the kind of work you want, a real experience that proves you enjoy it, and why now; answer "why this firm" with two specific, checked details linked to your own background. Interviewers have heard "I like solving problems" thousands of times. Specific, personal and evidenced is what makes you memorable.
body:
Why consulting: a three-part shape

  1. What draws you: one or two things about the work itself, such as solving unfamiliar problems across industries or helping leaders make big decisions.
  2. Evidence from your past: a moment when you did something similar and loved it. This is what makes the motivation believable.
  3. Why now: where you are in your career and what you want to build next.

Someone who enjoyed diagnosing customer churn in a product role, for example, might say they want broader exposure to business models and more ambiguous problems, alongside clients. The example carries the answer.

Why this firm: two checked details

Replace generalities with two details you can stand behind, and connect each to yourself:

  • People: who you spoke to and what struck you. Networking is how you get this.
  • Work: a practice, industry or type of project the firm is known for that matches your interests.
  • How it works: something about staffing, training or culture you heard from someone inside, not read in a brochure.

Be careful not to claim firms have completely different cultures based on marketing material alone. Interviewers know their firm better than you do.

Weak versus strong

Weak: "I love solving problems and working with smart people, and your firm is one of the most prestigious in the world."
Strong: "At university I led a project redesigning our hall's food waste process, and the part I loved was turning messy data into a decision people agreed on. Consulting would let me do that across many industries early in my career. I'm especially drawn to your healthcare work. When I spoke to Sam in your London office, she described a hospital operations project that's exactly the kind of problem I want to work on."

The weak answer could be said by anyone, to any firm. The strong one could only be said by this candidate, to this firm. Aim for about a minute. More strong and weak examples show the same contrast across different backgrounds.

What to avoid

  • Answers that fit any firm. If you could swap the firm's name for a competitor's, rewrite it.
  • Leading with money, prestige or exit opportunities. They may be true, but they say nothing about whether you will enjoy the job.
  • Criticising other firms. It reflects on you, not them.
  • A list of adjectives. "Collaborative, entrepreneurial, impactful" is not a reason.

Stress-test it with a friend

Say the answer aloud, then have a friend challenge every phrase: "Which experience proves that?" "Why couldn't you do that in your current role?" "What would you do at our firm that you couldn't do at another?" If you fall back on prestige or vague "learning opportunities", the motivation needs more work.

Try it now: what would you say to "Why not stay in your current job and move into strategy there?"

Show the answer

Acknowledge the option, then show what consulting gives that the alternative does not: "I've considered it, and I've done some strategy work in my current role. What I want now is to see many different businesses and problems quickly, with people who are very good at structuring them. That breadth is hard to get inside one company in the next few years." Then tie it back to your evidence.

Where to go next

This question often follows "tell me about yourself", so make the two answers consistent. Then prepare the rest of the set with our guide to common fit questions.
